set1.q: Which pair of toxins does enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli produce?
opts: Coagulase and murine toxin
Coagulase and murine toxin are Yersinia pestis virulence factors; enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli makes heat-labile and heat-stable toxins.
Heat-labile and heat-stable
Correct: enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli makes a heat-labile toxin and a heat-stable toxin, which promote secretion of fluid and electrolytes by the intestinal epithelium.
Shiga toxin and endotoxin
Shiga toxin is carried by enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli O157:H7 (from Shigella); the enterotoxigenic strain makes heat-labile and heat-stable toxins.
Exotoxin A and exoenzyme S
Exotoxin A and exoenzyme S are Pseudomonas aeruginosa virulence factors; enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli makes heat-labile and heat-stable toxins.

set1.q: What is the reservoir of Escherichia coli O157:H7?
opts: Pet turtles and reptiles
Pet turtles and other reptiles spread the animal salmonelloses; Escherichia coli O157:H7 lives in the intestines of cattle.
Rabbits and other mammals
Rabbits carry tularemia, rabbit fever; the reservoir of Escherichia coli O157:H7 is the intestines of cattle.
The intestines of cattle
Correct: the reservoir is the intestines of cattle; people are infected through contaminated beef, water and vegetables.
Wild rodents and fleas
Wild rodents and their fleas carry Yersinia pestis; Escherichia coli O157:H7 lives in the intestines of cattle.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: In the scheme for Gram-negative pathogens, which genus is the obligate anaerobe?
opts: Pseudomonas
Pseudomonas is on the aerobic branch, the rods that do not ferment carbohydrates; the obligate anaerobe in the scheme is Bacteroides.
Escherichia
Escherichia is a facultative anaerobe that ferments lactose; the obligate anaerobe in the scheme is Bacteroides.
Haemophilus
Haemophilus is a facultative anaerobe on the non-lactose-fermenting, oxidase-positive branch; the obligate anaerobe is Bacteroides.
Bacteroides
Correct: the obligate anaerobes branch of the Gram-negative rods holds Bacteroides; the aerobes include Pseudomonas, and the facultative anaerobes include Escherichia and Haemophilus.

mis.Escherichia: facultative anaerobe taken for an obligate one
mis.Haemophilus: facultative anaerobe taken for an obligate one

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: How does enteropathogenic Escherichia coli damage the intestine?
opts: Secretes heat-stable toxin
The heat-stable and heat-labile toxins belong to enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli; the enteropathogenic strain adheres and destroys microvilli.
Releases Shiga toxin into vessels
Shiga toxin damaging the endothelium is the enterohemorrhagic mechanism; enteropathogenic Escherichia coli adheres and destroys microvilli.
Adheres and destroys microvilli
Correct: the bacteria adhere to the intestinal lining and destroy the microvilli; they also inhibit the uptake of vitamin B1 (thiamin).
Invades the villi of the colon
Invading the villi of the large intestine is what Shigella does; enteropathogenic Escherichia coli adheres to the lining and destroys microvilli.

mis.Invades the villi of the colon: adjacent fact from the same lecture (Shigella)

set1.q: Which bacteria are actually more prevalent in the gut than Escherichia coli?
opts: Klebsiella and Enterobacter
Klebsiella and Enterobacter are other coliforms of the normal flora; the gut bacteria more prevalent than Escherichia coli are the anaerobes Bacteroides and Bifidobacterium.
Proteus and Providencia
Proteus and Providencia are noncoliform opportunists; the bacteria more prevalent than Escherichia coli are the anaerobes Bacteroides and Bifidobacterium.
Salmonella and Shigella
Salmonella and Shigella are true pathogens, not normal flora; the gut's more prevalent anaerobes are Bacteroides and Bifidobacterium.
Bacteroides and Bifidobacterium
Correct: Escherichia coli is the common aerobic, non-fastidious gut bacterium, but it is not the most prevalent; the anaerobic Bacteroides and Bifidobacterium are.

set1.q: What is the bubo of bubonic plague?
opts: A gangrenous patch of skin
Purpura that degenerates into necrosis and gangrene is septicemic plague; the bubo is a swollen, necrotic lymph node.
An ulcer at the bite site
An ulcerative skin lesion is a tularemia sign; the plague bubo is a swollen lymph node in the groin or axilla.

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Which metabolic profile fits Pseudomonas?
opts: Aerobic respiration, no fermentation
Correct: pseudomonads use aerobic respiration and do not ferment carbohydrates; they produce oxidase and catalase.
Ferments lactose, like coliforms
Lactose fermentation defines the coliform enterics; Pseudomonas does not ferment carbohydrates and relies on aerobic respiration.
Obligate anaerobic fermentation
The obligate anaerobe of the Gram-negative scheme is Bacteroides; Pseudomonas uses aerobic respiration.
Ferments glucose, oxidase negative
Glucose fermentation with a negative oxidase describes the Enterobacteriaceae; Pseudomonas does not ferment carbohydrates and produces oxidase.

set1.q: Which opportunist has multiple animal reservoirs and causes catheter-related urinary tract infections?
opts: Providencia species
Correct: Providencia has multiple animal reservoirs and causes nosocomial infections, urinary tract infections with catheters, and gastroenteritis.
Pasteurella multocida
Pasteurella is normal flora in animals, but it infects through animal bites and scratches, not catheters; the catheter opportunist with animal reservoirs is Providencia.
Klebsiella pneumoniae
Klebsiella pneumoniae is a normal inhabitant of the human respiratory tract, known for nosocomial pneumonia; the opportunist with animal reservoirs is Providencia.

set1.cite: Lecture 14  Dr. Webster Gram Negative Bacilli of Medical Importance.pptx, Slide 72, 66, 96 and 100

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Which traits do ALL members of the Enterobacteriaceae share?
opts: Catalase negative, spore-forming
Enterics are catalase positive and non-spore-forming small rods; all of them ferment glucose and are oxidase negative.
Ferment glucose, oxidase negative
Correct: all enterics ferment glucose, reduce nitrates to nitrites, are oxidase negative and catalase positive; they are facultative anaerobes that grow best in air.
Ferment lactose, oxidase positive
Lactose fermentation splits the coliforms from the non-coliforms, so not all enterics ferment it, and enterics are oxidase negative.
Obligate aerobes, oxidase positive
Obligate aerobes with oxidase describe Pseudomonas and its relatives; enterics are facultative anaerobes and oxidase negative.

mis.Ferment lactose, oxidase positive: dividing trait taken for a shared one
mis.Obligate aerobes, oxidase positive: adjacent fact from the same lecture (Pseudomonas)

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Which Escherichia coli pathotype produces Shiga toxin?
opts: Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli
Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli destroys microvilli and blocks thiamin uptake; Shiga toxin belongs to the enterohemorrhagic strain.
Enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli

Correct: enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli O157:H7, also called Shiga toxin-producing Escherichia coli, carries Shiga toxin into host cells through a cell wall receptor that fuses with the host membrane.
Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli
Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli makes heat-labile and heat-stable toxins, not Shiga toxin; Shiga toxin is the enterohemorrhagic strain's.
Enteroinvasive Escherichia coli
Enteroinvasive Escherichia coli has no toxins and damages the wall mechanically; Shiga toxin belongs to the enterohemorrhagic strain.

set1.q: Which pigment gives Pseudomonas aeruginosa its greenish-blue color?
opts: Pyocyanin
Correct: Pseudomonas aeruginosa produces the greenish-blue pigment pyocyanin, and it has a grapelike odor; many pseudomonads make water-soluble pigments.
Prodigiosin
Prodigiosin is the red pigment of Serratia marcescens; the greenish-blue pigment of Pseudomonas aeruginosa is pyocyanin.
Methylene blue
Methylene blue is a dye in eosin methylene blue agar, which selects for Gram-negative bacteria; the pigment of Pseudomonas aeruginosa is pyocyanin.
Crystal violet
Crystal violet is a selective agent in MacConkey's agar, not a bacterial pigment; Pseudomonas aeruginosa makes pyocyanin.

set1.q: Which Bordetella pertussis adhesion protein, long a vaccine component, is missing from newly developing strains?
opts: Pertactin

Exotoxin A is the Pseudomonas aeruginosa toxin that inhibits protein synthesis; the pertussis adhesion protein in vaccines is pertactin.
Porin OprH
OprH is a Pseudomonas aeruginosa porin membrane protein in a candidate Pseudomonas vaccine; the pertussis adhesion protein is pertactin.
Shiga toxin
Shiga toxin belongs to Shigella and enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli; the pertussis adhesion protein is pertactin.

opts: A human acellular vaccine

A human subunit vaccine

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Why can antibiotic therapy of a Gram-negative infection itself release endotoxin?
opts: The drug switches on toxin genes
Endotoxin is not a gene product switched on by the drug; it is the lipopolysaccharide already in the outer membrane, freed when the cells lyse.
The drug activates the lipid A
Lipid A is already the biologically active component; the drug does not activate it, it frees it by lysing the cells.
Dying cells secrete it to defend
Endotoxin is not secreted as a defense; it is a structural component of the outer membrane released as the cells break apart.
Killing the cells lyses them
Correct: endotoxin is part of the Gram-negative outer membrane and is released on the lysis of the cells, including lysis brought about by antibiotic therapy.

set1.q: Who are the hosts of Salmonella typhi?
opts: Humans exclusively
Correct: humans are the exclusive hosts of Salmonella typhi and Salmonella paratyphi, the most serious pathogens of the genus, causing typhoid and paratyphoid fever.
Poultry and their eggs
Poultry and eggs carry the animal salmonelloses such as Salmonella enteritidis; Salmonella typhi infects humans only.

Pet turtles and bearded dragons spread the animal salmonelloses; the hosts of Salmonella typhi are humans exclusively.

opts: Wasting infantile diarrhea

Hemolytic uremic syndrome is the kidney complication of enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli O157:H7; the enterotoxigenic strain causes traveler's diarrhea.

Bacillary dysentery is shigellosis, an invasive disease of the large intestine; the enterotoxigenic strain causes traveler's diarrhea.

set1.q: Which form of plague is highly contagious by aerosol?
opts: Pneumonic
Correct: in pneumonic plague the infection is localized to the lungs, highly contagious by aerosol infection, and fatal without treatment.
Bubonic
Bubonic plague starts in a flea bite and spreads through the lymph to form a bubo; the aerosol-spread form is pneumonic.
Septicemic
Septicemic plague is the progression to massive bacterial growth with purpura and gangrene; the aerosol-spread form is pneumonic.
Sylvatic
Sylvatic names plague caught from wild animals, a source rather than a clinical form; the aerosol-spread form is pneumonic.

set1.q: Which part of the bowel does enteroinvasive Escherichia coli inflame?
opts: The ileum
Inflammation of the ileum that mimics appendicitis is Yersinia enterocolitica; enteroinvasive Escherichia coli inflames the large intestine.
The large intestine
Correct: enteroinvasive Escherichia coli causes an inflammatory disease of the large intestine, similar to shigellosis.
The small intestine
Adhering to the small intestine by fimbriae is enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli; the enteroinvasive strain inflames the large intestine.
The gallbladder
The gallbladder is where chronic typhoid carriers shed Salmonella typhi from; enteroinvasive Escherichia coli inflames the large intestine.

mis.The gallbladder: adjacent fact from the same lecture (Salmonella)
mis.The ileum: adjacent fact from the same lecture (Yersinia)

set1.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set1.q: Which organism causes melioidosis?
opts: Burkholderia cepacia
Burkholderia cepacia is the plant pathogen and opportunist that troubles cystic fibrosis patients; melioidosis is Burkholderia pseudomallei.
Brucella abortus
Brucella abortus is the cattle species that causes brucellosis (undulant fever); melioidosis is Burkholderia pseudomallei.
Francisella tularensis
Francisella tularensis causes tularemia, rabbit fever; melioidosis is Burkholderia pseudomallei.
Burkholderia pseudomallei

Correct: Burkholderia pseudomallei, from the soil and water of tropical climates, causes melioidosis: wound infections with nodules, pneumonia, septicemia, endotoxic shock and liver and brain abscesses.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: How does enteroinvasive Escherichia coli damage the intestinal wall?
opts: Mechanically, without toxins
Correct: it binds the intestinal wall with adhesin proteins and damages it through mechanical cell damage; it produces no toxins.
With heat-labile toxin
The heat-labile and heat-stable toxins belong to enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli; the enteroinvasive strain makes no toxins.
Through Shiga toxin release
Shiga toxin belongs to enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli and Shigella; the enteroinvasive strain has no toxins and damages cells mechanically.
By blocking thiamin uptake
Inhibiting thiamin (vitamin B1) uptake is an enteropathogenic Escherichia coli effect; the enteroinvasive strain causes mechanical cell damage.
set2.cite: Lecture 14  Dr. Webster Gram Negative Bacilli of Medical Importance.pptx, Slide 57, 56, 58 and 59

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: From which organ do some chronic carriers shed Salmonella typhi?
opts: The gallbladder
Correct: typhoid has asymptomatic carriers, and some chronic carriers shed the bacilli from the gallbladder.
The lungs
Shedding from the lungs by aerosol is the pneumonic plague pattern; chronic typhoid carriers shed from the gallbladder.
The skin
Rose spots are a typhoid rash, not the carrier's source; chronic carriers shed Salmonella typhi from the gallbladder.
The kidneys
The kidneys are the target of hemolytic uremic syndrome, not a typhoid carrier site; chronic carriers shed from the gallbladder.

mis.The lungs: adjacent fact from the same lecture (pneumonic plague)
mis.The skin: symptom site taken for carriage site
mis.The kidneys: adjacent fact from the same lecture (EHEC)

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: How does Shigella cause dysentery?
opts: It perforates the bowel wall
Shigella does not perforate the intestine; perforation of the intestinal wall is a typhoid feature.
It sticks to small-bowel cells
Adhesion to the small intestine by fimbriae is enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli; Shigella invades the villi of the large intestine.
It invades the large-bowel villi
Correct: Shigella invades the villi of the large intestine and enters Peyer's patches to set off inflammation; it does not perforate the intestine or invade the blood.
It spreads into the bloodstream
Shigella does not invade the blood; it is Salmonella typhi whose invasive diarrhea leads to septicemia.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Why is septicemic plague called the black plague?
opts: Its buboes turn black
Buboes are the swollen nodes of bubonic plague; the black of septicemic plague is purpura degenerating into gangrene.
The bacteria make black pigment
Yersinia pestis makes no black pigment; the black comes from purpura that degenerates into necrosis and gangrene.
The lungs fill with dark blood
Lung involvement is the pneumonic form; the black of septicemic plague is gangrene of the skin after purpura.
Purpura turns to gangrene

Correct: in septicemic plague, massive bacterial growth and virulence factors cause intravascular coagulation, subcutaneous hemorrhage and purpura that degenerates into necrosis and gangrene, the black plague.
set2.cite: Lecture 14  Dr. Webster Gram Negative Bacilli of Medical Importance.pptx, Slide 88

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: How do the toxins of enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli cause diarrhea?
opts: Apoptosis of renal tubule cells
Apoptosis of renal tubular epithelial cells is the hemolytic uremic syndrome of enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli; the enterotoxigenic toxins drive fluid secretion.
Fluid and electrolyte secretion
Correct: the heat-labile and heat-stable toxins promote secretion of fluid and electrolytes in the intestinal epithelium, giving diarrhea, cramping and a low-grade to no fever.
Mechanical damage of the wall
Mechanical cell damage without toxins is how enteroinvasive Escherichia coli harms the wall; the enterotoxigenic toxins drive fluid and electrolyte secretion.
Destruction of microvilli
Destroying the microvilli is the enteropathogenic Escherichia coli mechanism; the enterotoxigenic toxins drive fluid and electrolyte secretion.
set2.cite: Lecture 14  Dr. Webster Gram Negative Bacilli of Medical Importance.pptx, Slide 56, 57, 58 and 60

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: What do the O157 and H7 in Escherichia coli O157:H7 name?
opts: Toxin and plasmid types
The letters name surface antigens, not a toxin or a plasmid; O157 is somatic and H7 flagellar.
Somatic and flagellar antigens
Correct: O157 is the somatic (O, cell wall) antigen type 157 and H7 the flagellar (H) antigen type 7.
Flagellar and capsule antigens
H is indeed the flagellar antigen, but O is the somatic (cell wall) antigen, not the capsule; the capsule antigen is K.
Capsule and somatic antigens
The capsule antigen is K, which this name does not use; O157 is the somatic antigen and H7 the flagellar antigen.

mis.Toxin and plasmid types: antigen naming confused with virulence factors

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: In water testing, what does a coliform count indicate?
opts: Tropical soil runoff
Tropical soil and water carry Burkholderia pseudomallei; a coliform count indicates fecal contamination in water.
Fecal contamination
Correct: the coliform count, with Escherichia coli the classic coliform, is the indicator of fecal contamination in water.
Legionella in the water
Legionella in water systems is found by culturing it on charcoal yeast extract agar; a coliform count indicates fecal contamination.
Biofilms on the pipes
Biofilms are how Pseudomonas and Stenotrophomonas persist on equipment; a coliform count indicates fecal contamination.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: The colonies on this plate have stained the agar greenish-blue. Which organism makes this pigment?
opts: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Correct: the greenish-blue color spreading through the agar is pyocyanin, the pigment of Pseudomonas aeruginosa; many pseudomonads make water-soluble pigments.
Serratia marcescens
Serratia marcescens makes a red pigment, prodigiosin, rather than a greenish-blue one; that pigment belongs to Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
Klebsiella pneumoniae
Klebsiella pneumoniae is recognized by its large capsule, not a pigment; the greenish-blue pigment is Pseudomonas aeruginosa's pyocyanin.
Proteus vulgaris
Proteus vulgaris is recognized by its wavelike swarming growth, not a pigment; greenish-blue agar points to Pseudomonas aeruginosa.

mis.Serratia marcescens: pigmented organism with the wrong color

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Which three properties are used to differentiate the Gram-negative bacilli?
opts: Spores, acid-fastness and capsule
These Gram-negative bacilli are non-spore-forming, and acid-fastness is not on the list; they are sorted by oxygen requirement, lactose fermentation and oxidase.
Catalase, coagulase and hemolysis
None of these three is a sorting property here (all enterics are catalase positive); the three are oxygen requirement, lactose fermentation and oxidase.
Shape, size and pigment
Pigment marks some species, such as the greenish-blue of Pseudomonas aeruginosa, but is not a sorting axis; the three are oxygen, lactose fermentation and oxidase.
Oxygen, lactose and oxidase
Correct: Gram-negative bacilli are differentiated by oxygen requirements (aerobic, facultatively anaerobic, obligate anaerobic), the ability to ferment lactose, and the oxidase enzyme.

mis.Shape, size and pigment: identifying traits taken as the scheme

set2.cite: Lecture 14  Dr. Webster Gram Negative Bacilli of Medical Importance.pptx, Slide 12, 13 and 46

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Why is antibiotic therapy approached with caution in enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli infection?
opts: It destroys the intestinal microvilli
Destroying microvilli is what enteropathogenic Escherichia coli itself does; the caution with antibiotics in enterohemorrhagic infection is that they may worsen hemolytic uremic syndrome.
It spreads the infection to the lungs
No spread to the lungs is described; the caution is that antibiotic therapy may exacerbate hemolytic uremic syndrome.
It triggers relapse from the gallbladder
Gallbladder shedding is how chronic typhoid carriers spread Salmonella typhi; for enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli, antibiotics may worsen hemolytic uremic syndrome.
It may worsen hemolytic uremic syndrome
Correct: antibiotic therapy may exacerbate hemolytic uremic syndrome; treatment relies on dialysis, transfusions and plasmapheresis, with corticosteroids if diarrhea is not involved.

mis.It triggers relapse from the gallbladder: adjacent fact from the same lecture (typhoid)

set2.cite: Lecture 14  Dr. Webster Gram Negative Bacilli of Medical Importance.pptx, Slide 63, 58 and 73

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Which stage of pertussis brings a recurrent persistent cough followed by a deep inhalation, the whoop?
opts: Septicemic
Septicemic is a form of plague, with massive bacterial growth, purpura and gangrene; the whooping stage of pertussis is paroxysmal.
Pneumonic
Pneumonic is the lung form of plague, spread by aerosol; the whooping stage of pertussis is paroxysmal.
Paroxysmal

Correct: in the paroxysmal stage, a recurrent persistent cough is followed by a deep inhalation, the whoop; the catarrhal stage before it brings nasal drainage, congestion, sneezing and an occasional cough.
Catarrhal
The catarrhal stage is the earlier one, with nasal drainage, congestion, sneezing and an occasional cough; the whoop belongs to the paroxysmal stage.

mis.Septicemic: adjacent fact from the same lecture (plague)
mis.Pneumonic: adjacent fact from the same lecture (plague)

set2.cite: Lecture 14  Dr. Webster Gram Negative Bacilli of Medical Importance.pptx, Slide 31 and 88

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: How is legionellosis transmitted?
opts: By inhaling aerosols
Correct: legionellosis is transmitted by aerosols from water sources such as cooling towers, spas, air conditioning and decorative fountains.
By drinking tap water
Tap water can harbor Legionella, but the disease is transmitted by aerosols, the spray from cooling towers, spas and fountains.
By tick and flea bites
No vector carries legionellosis; it is transmitted by aerosols from water sources.
By eating raw vegetables
Supermarket vegetable spraying systems are a source because they make aerosols; legionellosis is transmitted by inhaling aerosols, not by eating.
set2.cite: Lecture 14  Dr. Webster Gram Negative Bacilli of Medical Importance.pptx, Slide 40, 39 and 42

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Why is pertussis incidence highest among babies under 1 year old?
opts: Their boosters have worn off
Waning immunity after childhood vaccination drives the rise in older children and adolescents; the youngest infants have had no vaccine yet.
They receive a whole-cell vaccine
Infants are given the acellular DTaP (diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis) series, not a whole-cell vaccine; the highest incidence is in infants too young (under 2 months) to vaccinate.
They are too young to be vaccinated
Correct: average incidence is highest among children under 1 year because infants less than 2 months old cannot get vaccinated.
They are the main healthy carriers
The reservoir is apparently healthy carriers in general, not infants in particular; infants suffer most because the youngest cannot yet be vaccinated.

mis.They are the main healthy carriers: reservoir confused with the most affected

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Tularemia is also known by which name?
opts: Malta fever
Malta fever is another name for brucellosis; tularemia is rabbit fever, caused by Francisella tularensis.
Pontiac fever
Pontiac fever is one of the two illnesses Legionella causes; tularemia is rabbit fever.
Rabbit fever
Correct: tularemia, caused by Francisella tularensis, is rabbit fever, a zoonosis of mammals endemic to the northern hemisphere, particularly rabbits.
Undulant fever
Undulant fever is brucellosis, named for its fluctuating fever; tularemia is rabbit fever.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Which enteric is a true pathogen rather than a member of the normal flora?
opts: Salmonella typhi
Correct: Salmonella typhi is one of the true pathogenic enterics, with the shigellas and the enteric yersinias; Klebsiella, Enterobacter and Proteus belong to the normal flora.
Klebsiella pneumoniae
Klebsiella is a coliform of the normal flora (a normal inhabitant of the respiratory tract), important mainly as an opportunist; Salmonella typhi is a true pathogen.
Enterobacter species
Enterobacter is a coliform of the normal flora, an opportunist; the true pathogen among these is Salmonella typhi.
Proteus vulgaris
Proteus is a non-coliform of the normal flora, an opportunistic pathogen; the true pathogen among these is Salmonella typhi.

mis.Klebsiella pneumoniae: normal flora taken for a true pathogen
mis.Enterobacter species: normal flora taken for a true pathogen
mis.Proteus vulgaris: normal flora taken for a true pathogen

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Which genus produces the wavelike growth shown on this plate?
opts: Serratia
Serratia marcescens is recognized by its red pigment, prodigiosin; wavelike swarming is Proteus.
Haemophilus
Haemophilus is fastidious and needs chocolate agar; it does not swarm across a plate. Wavelike swarming is Proteus.
Proteus
Correct: the wavelike, swarming pattern is the diagnostic growth of Proteus vulgaris, a highly motile rod with peritrichous flagella.
Klebsiella
Klebsiella is recognized by its large capsule and is nonmotile in the biochemical tree; swarming growth is Proteus.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Which measure is given to prevent enteropathogenic Escherichia coli infection?
opts: Breast feeding
Correct: breast feeding is the prevention given for this wasting infantile diarrhea; treatment is fluid and electrolyte therapy.
A Haemophilus subunit vaccine
The subunit Hib vaccine protects against Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib); enteropathogenic Escherichia coli is prevented by breast feeding.
Quarantine and rodent control
Quarantine and rodent control prevent plague; enteropathogenic Escherichia coli is prevented by breast feeding.
Pasteurizing dairy
Avoiding unpasteurized dairy protects against brucellosis; enteropathogenic Escherichia coli is prevented by breast feeding.

set2.q: Which condition can Yersinia enterocolitica infection mimic?
opts: Shigellosis
Resembling shigellosis is said of enteroinvasive Escherichia coli; Yersinia enterocolitica's ileitis can mimic appendicitis.
Crohn's disease
An association with Crohn's disease is given for Proteus; Yersinia enterocolitica's ileitis can mimic appendicitis.
Typhoid fever
Typhoid fever is Salmonella typhi infection leading to septicemia; Yersinia enterocolitica can mimic appendicitis.
Appendicitis
Correct: the bacteria enter the small intestinal mucosa, some enter the lymphatics and survive in phagocytes, and inflammation of the ileum can mimic appendicitis.

set2.cite: Lecture 14  Dr. Webster Gram Negative Bacilli of Medical Importance.pptx, Slide 80, 57, 70 and 73

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: How does an infected flea pass Yersinia pestis to a new host?
opts: By injecting it from saliva glands
The bacteria multiply in the flea's gut, not its salivary glands; they are passed on in material the blocked flea regurgitates as it bites.
By leaving infected feces on skin
Plague is passed in regurgitated material during the bite, after coagulase blocks the flea's esophagus, not in its feces.
By laying eggs in the host's skin
Fleas do not pass plague through eggs in the skin; the blocked, ravenous flea regurgitates the bacteria while biting.
By regurgitating while it bites
Correct: the bacteria replicate in the flea's gut and coagulase clots the blood, blocking its esophagus; the ravenous flea bites more hosts and transmits the bacterium in regurgitated material.
set2.cite: Lecture 14  Dr. Webster Gram Negative Bacilli of Medical Importance.pptx, Slide 83 and image on Slide 84

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: The diagram shows enteric bacteria invading the intestinal epithelium, with bleeding. Which organism is the example of this invasive diarrheal disease?
opts: Shigella dysenteriae

Correct: invasive diarrheal disease, with bacteria entering the epithelium and causing bleeding, is exemplified by Shigella; the toxigenic pattern, an oversecretion of fluid, by enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli.
Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli
Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli is the example of TOXIGENIC disease, an oversecretion of fluid without invasion; the invasive example is Shigella.
Klebsiella pneumoniae
Klebsiella pneumoniae is a respiratory-tract coliform causing nosocomial pneumonia and urinary tract infection, not invasive diarrhea; that pattern is Shigella's.
Proteus vulgaris
Proteus vulgaris is an opportunist of urinary tract and wound infections, known for swarming; the invasive diarrhea example is Shigella.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Which change in the circulation marks warm shock, the early stage after a large flood of endotoxin?
opts: Resistance rises and output rises
Peripheral arterial resistance falls, not rises, as arteries and arterioles dilate; it is cardiac output that initially increases.
Arterioles dilate and output rises
Correct: arteries and arterioles dilate, peripheral arterial resistance falls and cardiac output initially increases, called warm shock; later cardiac output decreases and blood pressure falls.
Arterioles constrict and output falls
Constriction with falling output is not the early picture; in warm shock the vessels dilate and cardiac output initially increases.
Output falls and pressure drops
A falling cardiac output and blood pressure come later; warm shock is the earlier stage, when dilation lowers resistance and output initially rises.

mis.Output falls and pressure drops: later stage taken for the early one

set2.cite: Lecture 14  Dr. Webster Gram Negative Bacilli of Medical Importance.pptx, Slide 11

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Why is Haemophilus grown on chocolate agar?
opts: It is killed by bile salts
Bile salts are the selective agent of MacConkey's agar; chocolate agar is chosen because Haemophilus needs blood factors such as hemin.
It needs hemin from cooked blood
Correct: Haemophilus is fastidious, and none can grow on blood agar without special techniques; chocolate agar (cooked blood) supplies the hemin or nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide it requires.
It needs low oxygen to survive
The requirement is for blood factors (hemin, nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide or its phosphate), not low oxygen; chocolate agar is cooked blood.
It ferments the lactose in it
Lactose fermentation is read on MacConkey's and eosin methylene blue agar; chocolate agar is used because Haemophilus needs hemin from cooked blood.
set2.cite: Lecture 14  Dr. Webster Gram Negative Bacilli of Medical Importance.pptx, Slide 97 and 48

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Burkholderia cepacia is a particular problem in which patients?
opts: Those with cystic fibrosis
Correct: Burkholderia cepacia, a rapidly mutating, multidrug-resistant opportunist, is a particular problem in cystic fibrosis, where it is a copathogen with Pseudomonas.
Soldiers with combat wounds
Infections after traumatic combat wounds belong to Acinetobacter baumannii; Burkholderia cepacia is a particular problem in cystic fibrosis.
Patients on dialysis
Dialysis equipment is contaminated by Stenotrophomonas maltophilia biofilms; Burkholderia cepacia is a particular problem in cystic fibrosis.
Travelers to the tropics
Tropical soil and water carry Burkholderia pseudomallei, the cause of melioidosis; Burkholderia cepacia is a particular problem in cystic fibrosis.

set2.q: Which infection is typical of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in an otherwise healthy person?

Undulant fever is brucellosis, caught from infected animals or unpasteurized dairy products; Pseudomonas aeruginosa gives healthy people otitis externa.

Whooping cough is pertussis, caused by Bordetella pertussis; Pseudomonas aeruginosa gives healthy people swimmer's ear, skin rashes and urinary tract infection.
Rabbit fever
Rabbit fever is tularemia, caused by Francisella tularensis; Pseudomonas aeruginosa gives healthy people otitis externa.
Swimmer's ear
Correct: in healthy people it typically causes skin rashes, urinary tract infection, otitis externa (swimmer's ear) and corneal ulcers in contact lens wearers.

set2.q: Which rash marks typhoid fever?
opts: A follicular skin rash
Skin rashes in healthy people are typical of Pseudomonas aeruginosa; typhoid gives rose-colored spots.
Rose-colored spots
Correct: typhoid fever brings a sustained fever (103-104 degrees), a rash of rose-colored spots, weakness, stomach pains and loss of appetite.
Purpura with necrosis
Purpura that degenerates into necrosis and gangrene marks septicemic plague; typhoid gives rose-colored spots.
An ulcer with swollen nodes
Ulcerative skin lesions with swollen lymph nodes mark tularemia; typhoid gives a rash of rose-colored spots.

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: How is Pasteurella multocida usually acquired?
opts: Eating undercooked beef
Undercooked beef spreads Escherichia coli O157:H7; Pasteurella multocida enters through animal bites or scratches.
Animal bites or scratches

Correct: Pasteurella is a zoonotic genus, normal flora in animals; animal bites or scratches cause a local abscess that can spread to joints, bones and lymph nodes, mostly in veterinarians but also from domestic animals.
Bites from infected fleas
Flea bites spread plague; Pasteurella multocida enters through animal bites or scratches.
Inhaling cooling-tower mist
Cooling-tower aerosols spread Legionella; Pasteurella multocida enters through animal bites or scratches.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: The capsule stain shows rods ringed by large capsules, from a patient with nosocomial pneumonia. Which coliform is it?
opts: Enterobacter species
Enterobacter infects urinary tract, surgical wounds, spinal fluid, sputum and blood, but the large capsule belongs to Klebsiella pneumoniae.
Escherichia coli
Escherichia coli is the gut coliform behind most urinary tract infections; the large capsule in nosocomial pneumonia marks Klebsiella pneumoniae.
Klebsiella pneumoniae
Correct: Klebsiella pneumoniae has a large capsule, shown by a capsule stain, and is a cause of nosocomial pneumonia; it is a normal inhabitant of the respiratory tract.
Citrobacter species
Citrobacter is an opportunist of urinary tract infections and bacteremia, not known for a large capsule; that is Klebsiella pneumoniae.

set2.io: 2 — Describe the modes of transmission by which humans acquire Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Which foods transmit Escherichia coli O157:H7?
opts: Eggs from backyard flocks
Eggs and backyard flocks spread Salmonella; Escherichia coli O157:H7 spreads through contaminated beef, water and vegetables.
Contaminated beef, water, vegetables
Correct: from its reservoir in cattle intestines, Escherichia coli O157:H7 reaches people through contaminated beef, water and vegetables.
Raw oysters and other shellfish
Shellfish are not named for this strain; Escherichia coli O157:H7 comes from cattle and reaches people in contaminated beef, water and vegetables.
Honey given to young infants
Honey is not a source named for any Gram-negative bacillus here; Escherichia coli O157:H7 spreads through contaminated beef, water and vegetables.

set2.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the morphology, medium, laboratory tests, biochemical reactions, diseases, clinical manifestations, methods of treatment, and prevention of Gram-negative bacilli of medical importance
set2.q: Which component of the Gram-negative lipopolysaccharide is its biologically active part?
opts: Core polysaccharide
The core polysaccharide is identical for large groups of bacteria and links lipid A to the O antigen; the biologically active part is lipid A.
Peptidoglycan
Peptidoglycan is the cell wall layer beneath the outer membrane, not part of the lipopolysaccharide; the active component of endotoxin is lipid A.
Lipid A
Correct: lipid A is the biologically active component of the lipopolysaccharide complex, the part most responsible for pathogenesis.
O antigen
The O antigen is the outer polysaccharide, unique for each organism; it identifies the organism, while the biologically active component is lipid A.

mis.O antigen: adjacent part of the molecule (identity marker)
mis.Peptidoglycan: wall layer confused with the lipopolysaccharide

set2.q: How do humans usually acquire brucellosis?
opts: From person-to-person droplets
Human-to-human transmission of brucellosis is rare; it comes from infected animals and their unpasteurized dairy products.
From the bite of an infected flea
Flea bites transmit plague; brucellosis comes from contact with infected animals' blood, urine or placentas, or unpasteurized dairy.
From aerosols of cooling towers
Cooling-tower aerosols transmit Legionella; brucellosis comes from infected animals or unpasteurized dairy products.
From infected animals or raw dairy

Correct: brucellosis is a zoonosis of animal handling and slaughtering, spread by contact with the blood, urine or placentas of infected animals or by unpasteurized dairy products; human-to-human spread is rare.
